## The Research-Production Gap

- Reffers to the disparity between the development of ML models during the research phase and their successful deployment. 

- For the adoption of machine learning by a company to deliver maximum value, it is necessary to carry out an efficient deployment.

- The systematic planning of a machine learning project’s lifecycle serves as a crucial workflow for ensuring successful implementation.

::: {.notes}
The gap between research and production is a significant challenge. 

We need to understand the differences between those environments. What are the actual targets, requirements and limitations.

:::

## Production x Research Environments

- Different focus

    - Research usually focus on models performance 

    - Production focus on the model serving side

- Different performance requirements

- Run on different devices

- Distinct compute requirements

::: {.notes}
Production and research environments have different focuses, performance requirements, 
and run on different devices. 

The production environment demands faster deployment, 
changes frequently, and deals with noisy data. Models are deployed on various devices, 
each with distinct compute requirements.
:::

## Production x Research Environments

- The production environment requires a faster deployment

- The production environment changes frequently

- Models are deployed in different devices

- Data is usually noisy 

::: {.notes}
In production enviroment we need to be aware of other software components in the system.
:::

## Production Environment

- In production, ML models are surrounded by software infrastructure. 

- Machine Learning code is a small fraction of the overall system.

In the production environment, machine learning models are just a 
part of the larger software infrastructure. 

Machine learning code  represents a small fraction of the overall system, surrounded by

examples:

To tackle the similar problem related to development, testing and continuous deployment, in the software engineering, field we have the Devops Culture. 

:::

##  DevOps Solution

- DevOps is called a "culture" because it represents a set of practices and principles that extend beyond just tools and technologies.

- The "Devops Culture" is heavily applied in software development teams.

- Definition: Set of practices for colaboration, developing, testing, deploying, and operating large-scale software systems. 

- DevOps culture is not limited to specific industries or technologies. It is a mindset that can benefit any organization seeking to improve software development and delivery processes. 

::: {.notes}
In software engineering, there is the devops solution... 

DevOps, which stands for Development and Operations, is a set of practices for collaboration, development, 
testing, deployment, and operation of large-scale software systems.

This culture can greatly benefit any 
organization looking to improve software development and delivery processes.

But what about machine learning systems? Can They be treated as software systems? 
:::

## DevOps Solution

- But machine learning systems have some extra complexity due to randomness, hyperperameters, changes in data and experimentation.

- The machine learning life-cycle envolves experimentation

::: {.notes}
However, machine learning systems introduce additional complexity due to Randomness, hyperparameters, 
changing data, and experimentation. 

The machine learning lifecycle involves ongoing experimentation. We have to "adapt" the solution. 
:::


## MLOps

- Definition: MLOps, short for Machine Learning Operations, is a set of practices and tools that aim to streamline and automate the deployment, monitoring, and management of machine learning (ML) models in production.

- MLOps is a structured approach to manage the end-to-end developing, deploying and mantaining Machine learning models.

- Improves the model management, deployment speed and quality control.

::: {.notes}
This is where MLOps comes into play. MLOps, or Machine Learning Operations, encompasses a set of practices 
and tools that streamline and automate the deployment, monitoring, and management of machine learning models 
in production. 

MLOps provides a structured approach to manage the end-to-end development, deployment, and maintenance of 
machine learning models.

MLOps can be classified also as a "culture" in the organization.

:::

## MLOps

- The MLOps lifecycle emphasizes collaboration between data scientists, machine learning engineers, DevOps teams, and domain experts. 

- By following this structured approach, companies can delivery the full potential of machine learning while minimizing risks and operational challenges.

- Frequently requires a set of open source software for the implementation.

::: {.notes}

It emphasizes collaboration between data scientists, machine learning engineers, 
DevOps teams, and domain experts. By following this structured approach, companies can unlock the full 
potential of machine learning while minimizing risks and operational challenges.

DevOps and MLOps have a lot of similarities

:::

## MLOps x DevOps

Similarities

- Source control

- Hybrid teams

- Unit tests

- Integration tests

- Continuous delivery

- Design patterns

::: {.notes}

DevOps and MLOps have some differences.

:::

## MLOps x DevOps 

- MLOps is experimental by nature.

- Testing (software and models)

- Automated Deploy (software and models)

::: {.notes}
MLOps is inherently experimental, involving testing and automated deployment. This is where it 
shares common ground with DevOps, which emphasizes source control, hybrid teams, unit tests, 
integration tests, continuous delivery, and design patterns.
:::

## MLOps x DevOps

- Monitoring (software and model performance)  

- Model Degradation

    - Discrepancy between training data and production environment data.

    - Change of data between training and prediction.  

::: {.notes}
However, challenges like model degradation, concept drift, and data drift set MLOps apart. 
Model degradation refers to the discrepancy between training data and production environment data, 
and the changes that occur between the training and prediction phases. Effective monitoring is 
critical in addressing these issues.

Its important to understand how to implement MLOps in one organization.

:::


## MLOps

- MLOps is not a one-size-fits-all approach.

- It can vary depending on the specific needs and requirements of an organization. 

- It helps bridge the gap between the development and operational aspects of machine learning.

- Allows companies to deploy and maintain models at scale effectively.

::: {.notes}
It's essential to understand that MLOps is not a one-size-fits-all approach. 

It's necessary to understand the needs for each company. 

It serves as a bridge between the development and operational aspects of machine learning, allowing companies to deploy and maintain 
models at scale effectively.

The MLOps implemented can vary depending on the level of automation.

:::

## Levels of Automation

- The level of automation of the Data, ML Model, and Code pipelines reflects the maturity of the ML process

- The target is to automate the ML-workflow steps without any intervention

- The three levels of automation:

    - Manual process

    - ML pipeline automation

    - CI/CD pipeline automation

::: {.notes}
Automation is a key aspect of MLOps, and the level of automation reflects the maturity of 
the machine learning process. The goal is to automate the ML workflow steps without manual 
intervention. This involves three levels of automation: manual processes, ML pipeline automation, 
and CI/CD pipeline automation.

Now we know the formal definitions and benefits of MLOps. Let's understand the continuous lifecycle.
:::

## MLOps - Phases

- MLOps practices can be divided in 4 bigger phases  

    - Scoping 

    - Data Collection
    
    - Modeling
    
    - Model Serving and Monitoring

::: {.notes}
MLOps can be divided into four major phases: Scoping, Data Collection, Modeling, and Model Serving and Monitoring.
:::

## Scoping

- Business Objectives and Problem Definition

- Do we really need Machine learning ?

- Who is the target audience ?

- Business understanding

- Project setup

::: {.notes}
The Scoping phase involves answering critical questions like "Do we really need machine learning?" 
and defining business objectives, project constraints, and timelines. We also assess data needs and 
required infrastructure.
:::

## Scoping

- Data Assessment

- Required Infrastructure

- Performance constraints

- Project constraints

## Concept and Data Drift

- Main factors:
    - Concept Drift 

    - Data Drift

::: {.notes}
Model degradation can result from concept drift, where the relationship between inputs 
and outputs changes over time, and data drift, which occurs when input data changes. 
Monitoring is crucial to address these issues.
:::

## Concept Drift

- The relationship between the model inputs and outputs changes overtime

- The model is not aware of this change

- Usually this change happens due to external factors

## Data Drift

- The change occurs when the model data input changes

- Usually happens due to an increased relevance of “under-learned” segments. 

## Concept and Data Drift

![](files/drift.png)

## Data Drift

- The change occurs when the model data input changes

- Usually happens due to an increased relevance of “under-learned” segments. 

## Data Drift 

- Statistical statistical measures to compare past and current features: 
    - Mean/median 

    - Standard deviation
    
    - Minimum and maximum values
    
    - Correlations

## Data Drift

- For continuous values, one can use distances and/or hypothesis tests such as:
    - Kullback–Leibler Distance

    - Kolmogorov-Smirnov Test
    
    - Population Stability Index (PSI)
    
    - Hellinger Distance.

## Data Drift 

- For categorical variables, you can use the chi-square test, entropy, cardinality or frequency of the feature.

- If there are many features, we can use some dimensionality reduction technique.
